description: Find the single habit that cascades into the others. Exercise improves sleep, sleep improves diet, diet improves mood. List five changes you want, determine which one makes the rest easier, and start there, only there, until the cascade confirms itself.

steps.description: List the five behavior changes you most want to make, stated as specific daily or weekly actions rather than vague goals.

inputs.name: current-life-friction
inputs.desc: The parts of daily life that feel hardest or most frustrating right now

inputs.name: improvement-wishlist
inputs.desc: Everything you wish you did more of or less of, without filtering

outputs.name: five-candidate-changes
outputs.desc: Exactly five behavior changes, each stated as a concrete observable action with a frequency

outputs.name: change-effort-notes
outputs.desc: For each change, a note on how hard it has felt to sustain in the past

process: Write down every behavior you wish you did more of or less of. Do not filter or rank yet. Include changes you have tried and abandoned before.
Reduce the list to the five that would matter most to your daily life. State each as an action a camera could record, such as walk thirty minutes after lunch, not get in shape.
For each of the five, note how many times you have tried it before and what made it stop. Past friction is data, not failure.
Confirm all five are things you could start this week with no new equipment, money, or permission. Changes that require a precondition belong on a later list.

steps.description: Map which of the five changes make the others easier, so you can see the causal structure instead of treating the five as independent.

inputs.name: change-effort-notes
inputs.desc: Past sustain history for each change

outputs.name: cascade-link-map
outputs.desc: A directed map where an arrow from A to B means doing A makes B easier or more automatic

outputs.name: downstream-count-per-change
outputs.desc: For each change, how many of the other four it sits upstream of

process: Take each pair of changes and ask one question: if I did the first consistently, would the second get easier, more likely, or more automatic? If yes, draw an arrow from the first to the second.
Trace the known physiological chains. Regular movement tends to improve sleep quality, better sleep tends to steady appetite and food choices, and steadier eating tends to lift mood and energy.
Count the outgoing arrows for each change. A change with three arrows out sits upstream of three other changes and is a cascade candidate.
Flag any change with zero outgoing arrows. It may still be worth doing, but it will not pull the others along and is not a keystone.

steps.description: Choose the one keystone habit by weighing cascade reach against how readily you could actually adopt it.

inputs.name: cascade-link-map
inputs.desc: The directed map of which changes drive which

outputs.name: chosen-keystone
outputs.desc: The single habit you will start with, chosen for high cascade reach and realistic adoptability

outputs.name: keystone-pick-rationale
outputs.desc: A short written reason tying the choice to its downstream effects and your ability to start it

process: Score each change on cascade reach using its downstream count, then score it on adoptability from one to ten, where a change you have failed at repeatedly scores low.
Score each change on feedback speed. A habit that produces a felt reward within an hour, such as a walk, builds itself faster than one whose payoff takes weeks.
Multiply reach by adoptability by feedback speed. The highest product is your keystone. If two tie, take the one you are more confident you can actually start.
Write one paragraph naming the keystone, the changes you expect it to pull along, and why you can begin it this week.

steps.description: Build a plan that starts the keystone habit and nothing else, so attention is not split across all five changes at once.

inputs.name: keystone-pick-rationale
inputs.desc: The reason this habit was chosen

outputs.name: keystone-start-plan
outputs.desc: A thirty-day plan that establishes the keystone at a small, repeatable size

outputs.name: single-focus-guardrail
outputs.desc: A written rule to not add any of the other four changes until the keystone is stable

process: Define the smallest version of the keystone that still counts, such as a ten-minute walk rather than a planned workout. The size must be low enough that skipping it would feel absurd.
Set a fixed time and place for the habit and remove one friction point in advance, such as leaving shoes by the door the night before.
Write the single-focus guardrail in plain words: you will not start the other four changes until the keystone has held for the full thirty days. Splitting focus is what stalled past attempts.
Name the first downstream change you expect to shift on its own. This becomes the signal that the cascade has started.

steps.description: Track the downstream behaviors without trying to change them, so you can tell whether the keystone is doing the work.

outputs.name: downstream-signal-tracker
outputs.desc: A simple daily log of the keystone plus the downstream behaviors you are not actively changing

outputs.name: cascade-check-dates
outputs.desc: The dates at day fifteen and day thirty when you will read the tracker for cascade effects

process: Log the keystone each day as done or not done. Keep the record binary so it takes seconds and you never skip logging.
Alongside it, note the downstream behaviors from the map, such as hours slept or servings of vegetables, as plain observations. Do not try to improve them.
Set two read dates, day fifteen and day thirty. Reading the log daily invites tinkering. Reading it on fixed dates keeps the test clean.
Record energy or mood in one word each evening. Mood often shifts before the measurable behaviors do and is an early cascade signal.

steps.description: After thirty days, read the tracker and decide whether the keystone produced the expected cascade or whether the causal map was wrong.

outputs.name: cascade-outcome-summary
outputs.desc: A summary of which downstream behaviors improved, held, or worsened over the thirty days

outputs.name: keystone-next-step
outputs.desc: The decision to continue and deepen the keystone, or to re-map the cascade if it did not appear

process: Count the days the keystone held. A keystone that held fewer than twenty of thirty days was not adopted firmly enough to test the cascade, so the first fix is the habit itself.
Compare each downstream behavior to its starting point. Two or more improving without deliberate effort confirms the cascade is real.
If the cascade appeared, keep the keystone and let the downstream changes deepen for another sixty days before adding the next change.
If it did not appear while the keystone held, the causal map was wrong. Return to the mapping step and pick a different upstream habit.

description: Redesign your environment so the behavior you want is the default and the behavior you want to drop takes effort. Willpower depletes across a day, so reduce friction for what you want to increase and stack three or four friction points against what you want to decrease.

steps.description: Name one behavior to increase and one to decrease, each stated as an observable action rather than a feeling or outcome.

inputs.name: behavior-to-increase
inputs.desc: Something you want to do more often but keep skipping

inputs.name: behavior-to-decrease
inputs.desc: Something you want to do less often but keep returning to

outputs.name: defined-increase-target
outputs.desc: The increase behavior stated as an action with a weekly minimum

outputs.name: defined-decrease-target
outputs.desc: The decrease behavior stated as an action with a weekly maximum

process: State the increase behavior as something a camera could record, such as read ten pages before bed, and attach a weekly minimum.
State the decrease behavior the same way, such as open the delivery app, and attach a weekly maximum rather than zero. Absolute bans create one failure that ends the effort.
Confirm both are single behaviors. Pairing a vague cluster like eat better with a single action makes the design impossible to aim.
Write why each matters in one sentence so the design has a reason to survive the first hard week.

steps.description: Count how many steps each behavior currently takes to start, because the step count is what willpower has to overcome every time.

outputs.name: increase-friction-points
outputs.desc: Every step between the current moment and starting the increase behavior

outputs.name: decrease-friction-points
outputs.desc: Every cue and step that currently makes the decrease behavior easy to start

process: Walk through starting the increase behavior and count each step. If a home workout needs finding clothes, clearing space, and locating a video, that is three friction points standing in the way.
Walk through the decrease behavior and count how few steps it takes. A behavior you can start in one tap has almost no friction protecting you from it.
Note the cue for each behavior. Most behaviors begin with something you see, so write down what you see right before each one starts.
Record the time of day each behavior tends to happen. Willpower is lowest late in the day, so late behaviors need environmental help the most.

steps.description: Cut the friction on the increase behavior down to one step or zero, so starting it no longer requires a decision.

inputs.name: increase-friction-points
inputs.desc: The steps currently blocking the increase behavior

outputs.name: friction-removal-plan
outputs.desc: Specific changes that reduce the increase behavior to a one-step or zero-step start

outputs.name: default-path-change
outputs.desc: One change that makes the increase behavior the automatic path rather than a choice

process: For each friction point, decide how to remove it in advance. Lay out clothes the night before, keep the book on the pillow, prefill the water bottle.
Aim for a one-step start. The goal is that beginning the behavior takes a single visible action rather than a chain of small decisions.
Change one default so the behavior happens unless you stop it. A fruit bowl at eye level and the snacks out of sight makes the good choice the lazy choice.
Pick a trigger you already encounter daily and attach the behavior to it, so the environment reminds you instead of your memory.

steps.description: Stack three or four friction points against the decrease behavior, because a single obstacle is usually not enough to interrupt an automatic habit.

inputs.name: decrease-friction-points
inputs.desc: The cues and steps that make the decrease behavior easy

outputs.name: friction-addition-stack
outputs.desc: A stack of three to four obstacles placed between you and the decrease behavior

outputs.name: friction-point-count
outputs.desc: The count of obstacles in the stack, confirmed to be at least three

process: Remove the cue first. Delete the app from the home screen, move the snack to a closed high cabinet, take the television remote out of the room.
Add steps to starting the behavior. Logging out after each use, unplugging a device, or storing a trigger item in another room each add a decision point.
Insert a delay rule, such as waiting ten minutes before acting on the urge. The urge often passes inside that window.
Count the obstacles and confirm there are at least three. One obstacle is cleared without thought. Three or four force a conscious choice each time.

steps.description: Make every environment change in a single session, because a gradual rollout lets the old cues persist and the design never takes hold.

outputs.name: environment-reset-checklist
outputs.desc: A single checklist of every physical and digital change to make in one sitting

outputs.name: reset-completion-record
outputs.desc: A record of which changes were actually completed during the session

process: Combine both plans into one checklist split into physical changes and digital changes, so you can move through the home and the phone in order.
Block thirty to sixty minutes and make every change at once. A design rolled out over a week leaves old cues in place long enough to win.
Check off each item as you complete it, and note any you could not finish, such as a change that needs a household member to agree.
Take a photo or written snapshot of the finished environment so you can restore it later when things drift back.

steps.description: After two and six weeks, check whether the behaviors actually shifted and adjust the friction where the design did not hold.

outputs.name: behavior-shift-results
outputs.desc: Actual frequency of each behavior over the review period against its target

outputs.name: friction-adjustment-list
outputs.desc: Friction to keep, friction to strengthen, and new cues discovered that need removing

process: Tally each behavior daily through the review period. Keep the tally simple enough that you never skip it.
At two weeks, compare each behavior to its target. A behavior within reach of target means the design worked. A behavior unchanged means a cue was missed or the friction stack was too shallow.
For any unchanged decrease behavior, hunt for the cue you did not remove. There is almost always a path you left open.
At six weeks, behaviors that held are becoming automatic. Redirect attention to the ones still struggling and deepen their friction design.

description: Build habits from identity first and behavior second. The aim is not to run but to become a runner, because each consistent action is a vote for the person you are becoming. Small actions repeated reliably outweigh large actions done once.

steps.description: Write the identity you want to hold rather than the outcome you want to reach, because behaviors that match an identity last and behaviors chasing an outcome fade.

inputs.name: goal-area
inputs.desc: The area of life you want to change, such as fitness, reading, or diet

inputs.name: who-you-want-to-become
inputs.desc: The kind of person you would like to be in that area

outputs.name: identity-statement
outputs.desc: A present-tense identity statement such as I am the kind of person who moves every day

outputs.name: identity-evidence-gap
outputs.desc: The gap between that identity and what your current actions would prove to an observer

process: Rewrite the goal as an identity. I want to run becomes I am a runner. I want to read more becomes I am a reader. The identity is the target, the behavior is the proof.
State the identity in the present tense and in plain words. A future-tense identity keeps the person you want to be permanently out of reach.
Ask what an observer would conclude you are from your actions this past month. The distance between that and your statement is the evidence gap.
Confirm the identity is about process, not achievement. I am a runner survives a slow week. I am a marathon finisher ends the day the race is over.

steps.description: List the small actions that would prove the identity, then find the smallest one you could not plausibly skip.

inputs.name: identity-evidence-gap
inputs.desc: The gap between identity and current actions

outputs.name: proving-actions
outputs.desc: A set of small actions, each of which an observer would read as evidence of the identity

outputs.name: smallest-vote-action
outputs.desc: The smallest single action from the set that still clearly counts as a vote for the identity

process: List actions a person with this identity would take, from small to large. A reader keeps a book nearby, reads one page, reads a chapter, finishes a book a week.
Mark which actions an outside observer would read as proof of the identity. Private intentions are not votes. Visible actions are.
Find the smallest action that still counts as a vote, such as reading a single page. The size must survive a tired, busy day.
Confirm the smallest action needs no motivation to complete. If it still feels like a decision on a bad day, make it smaller.

steps.description: Design how often you cast the vote, choosing consistency over intensity because the tally is what shapes the identity.

inputs.name: smallest-vote-action
inputs.desc: The smallest action that still counts

outputs.name: vote-schedule
outputs.desc: How often and when you will perform the smallest action, favoring daily over occasional

outputs.name: consistency-over-intensity-rule
outputs.desc: A written rule that a small action done daily beats a large action done rarely

process: Choose a frequency you can hit on your worst week, not your best. Daily small beats weekly large because it casts more votes and never lets the identity go quiet.
Attach the action to a fixed time or an existing routine so the vote has a reliable slot rather than depending on remembering.
Write the consistency rule plainly: showing up small is a vote, and a missed perfect day is worth less than a completed tiny one.
Decide what the minimum vote looks like on a terrible day, so even then the identity gets a mark in its favor.

steps.description: Set up a tally of votes so the identity has visible, accumulating evidence rather than a feeling that can be argued away.

inputs.name: vote-schedule
inputs.desc: The frequency and timing of the action

outputs.name: vote-tracker
outputs.desc: A simple running tally where each completed action is one recorded vote

outputs.name: vote-tally-method
outputs.desc: The rule for what earns a mark and how the total is read as evidence

process: Pick a tracker you will actually use, such as a calendar mark or a single tally line. The record must be faster to update than to skip.
Define what earns a mark. Completing the smallest vote action earns one, regardless of how the day otherwise went.
Keep the running total visible. A growing chain of votes becomes evidence you can point to when the identity feels false.
Do not record quality grades. The tally counts votes, not performance, because the identity is built by frequency, not by any single strong day.

steps.description: Surface competing identities that pull against the new one, because a habit fails fastest when it fights an identity you still hold.

outputs.name: conflicting-identity-list
outputs.desc: The existing identities that contradict the new one and the situations where they take over

outputs.name: conflict-resolution-plan
outputs.desc: How to reframe or contain each conflicting identity so it stops casting opposing votes

process: Name the identities that contradict the new one. A person building I eat well may still hold I am someone who treats myself when stressed.
Find the situations where the old identity takes over. Conflicts cluster around specific triggers such as stress, social settings, or fatigue.
Reframe the old identity rather than fighting it head on. I am someone who handles stress well can replace I treat myself when stressed, keeping the need but changing the action.
For situations you cannot reframe yet, plan to avoid or change the context so the old identity is not handed the vote by default.

steps.description: Review the vote tally to judge how firmly the identity has formed and choose the next identity to build.

outputs.name: identity-strength-assessment
outputs.desc: A judgment of how settled the identity is, based on vote count and whether it now feels true

outputs.name: next-identity-target
outputs.desc: The next identity to begin building, or a decision to deepen the current one

process: Read the vote count. A long unbroken tally means the identity has evidence behind it even on days it does not feel true.
Ask whether the behavior has started to feel like who you are rather than something you make yourself do. That shift is the real marker of a formed identity.
If the identity is settled, you can scale the action upward or begin a second identity. If it is still fragile, keep the vote small and protect the streak.
Choose the next identity so it reinforces the first rather than competing with it, so the identities stack rather than split your attention.

description: Attach a new habit to an existing one using the formula after I do a current habit I will do the new habit. The existing habit is the trigger, the new habit starts under two minutes, and the size scales only after the trigger fires reliably.

steps.description: Inventory the existing habits that already happen reliably every day, since only a reliable habit can serve as a trigger.

inputs.name: new-habit-goal
inputs.desc: The new habit you want to establish

inputs.name: daily-routine-description
inputs.desc: A walk through a normal day from waking to sleeping

outputs.name: reliable-anchor-habits
outputs.desc: Existing habits that happen at the same time and place almost every day

outputs.name: anchor-reliability-ratings
outputs.desc: A reliability rating for each candidate anchor, from rock solid to occasional

process: List the things you already do every day without deciding to, such as making coffee, brushing teeth, sitting down at your desk, or locking the door.
Keep only the ones that happen at a consistent time and place. A habit that floats around the day cannot anchor a new one.
Rate each anchor on reliability. An anchor you complete every single day is strong. One you skip on weekends is weak and will leave gaps.
Note the exact moment each anchor ends, because that ending is where the new habit will attach.

steps.description: Shrink the new habit to a version that takes under two minutes, because a tiny habit fires before resistance can build.

inputs.name: new-habit-goal
inputs.desc: The new habit you want to establish

outputs.name: tiny-habit-version
outputs.desc: The new habit reduced to an action that takes under two minutes

outputs.name: two-minute-check
outputs.desc: Confirmation that the tiny version can be completed in under two minutes on any day

process: Take the full habit and find the smallest first action. Do thirty minutes of yoga becomes unroll the mat. Read every night becomes open the book and read one page.
Strip the tiny version down until it takes under two minutes. The point is to establish the firing of the habit, not the full effort.
Confirm the tiny version requires no setup, decision, or willpower on a bad day. If it still feels like work, shrink it again.
Resist adding the full effort yet. The tiny version is the entire habit for now, and trying to do more early is what breaks the chain.

steps.description: Write the explicit stacking formula that binds the tiny habit to the chosen anchor so the trigger is unambiguous.

outputs.name: stack-formula
outputs.desc: A single sentence of the form after I do the anchor I will do the tiny habit

outputs.name: anchor-match-rationale
outputs.desc: Why this anchor fits this habit in time, place, and theme

process: Write the formula in one sentence: after I do the anchor, I will do the tiny habit. Name both parts exactly, with no vagueness about when.
Match the anchor to the habit by location and theme. A kitchen anchor fits a water or vitamin habit. A desk anchor fits a planning habit.
Confirm the anchor ends in the same place the new habit begins, so there is no travel or transition that gives resistance a gap to enter.
Write why the pairing fits. A mismatched pairing, such as attaching stretching to an anchor that happens while rushing out the door, will not hold.

steps.description: Test the stack in real days to check that the anchor actually leads into the new habit at the chosen moment.

outputs.name: placement-test-result
outputs.desc: Whether the new habit actually followed the anchor during a short trial

outputs.name: timing-fit-notes
outputs.desc: Notes on whether the moment was too rushed, too tired, or well placed

process: Run the stack for several days exactly as written and observe whether the anchor pulled the new habit along without a reminder.
Watch for the common failure: the anchor fires but the moment after it is rushed or crowded, so the new habit gets skipped.
If the habit keeps getting skipped, the placement is wrong even if the anchor is reliable. Move the habit to a calmer anchor rather than trying harder.
Note whether the anchor itself is as reliable in practice as you rated it. An anchor that slips on some days needs a backup anchor.

steps.description: Track the stack over a window long enough to tell whether the trigger fires reliably before any scaling happens.

inputs.name: placement-test-result
inputs.desc: The result of the short trial

outputs.name: reliability-tracker
outputs.desc: A daily record of whether the anchor fired and whether the habit followed

outputs.name: trigger-firing-rate
outputs.desc: The percentage of days the habit followed the anchor over the window

process: Track two things each day: did the anchor happen, and did the habit follow. Separating them tells you whether failures come from the anchor or the stack.
Run the window for at least two weeks. A trigger needs repetition before it becomes automatic, and a few good days are not proof.
Compute the firing rate as the share of days the habit followed the anchor. Treat anything under eighty percent as not yet reliable.
If the anchor often fails to happen at all, swap it for a more reliable anchor rather than blaming the new habit.

steps.description: Decide whether to scale the habit beyond its tiny version, which is allowed only once the trigger fires reliably.

inputs.name: reliability-tracker
inputs.desc: The daily record of anchor and habit

inputs.name: trigger-firing-rate
inputs.desc: The share of days the habit followed the anchor

outputs.name: scale-up-plan
outputs.desc: A plan to grow the habit gradually, triggered only by a reliable firing rate

outputs.name: next-stack-candidate
outputs.desc: The next tiny habit to stack once this one is stable, if desired

process: Scale only when the firing rate holds above eighty percent for two weeks. Scaling an unreliable trigger breaks the habit you were building.
Grow the habit in small increments, adding a little effort at a time, so the trigger keeps firing as the size increases.
If scaling causes the firing rate to drop, step back to the smaller size. The reliable small habit is worth more than a large one you skip.
Once the first stack is stable, pick the next tiny habit and attach it to the end of this one, building a chain one reliable link at a time.

description: Find the smallest intervention that still produces the result. Cardio needs about one hundred fifty minutes a week, strength needs two sessions a week, flexibility needs about ten minutes a day. Start at the minimum and increase only when you are below target, because sustainability beats intensity.

steps.description: Select the specific health outcomes you are aiming for and name the measure that tells you whether each is met.

inputs.name: health-goals
inputs.desc: What you want from your health, such as endurance, strength, mobility, or weight stability

inputs.name: current-activity-baseline
inputs.desc: What you currently do in a typical week

outputs.name: selected-targets
outputs.desc: The two or three outcomes you will actually pursue, kept few enough to sustain

outputs.name: target-metrics
outputs.desc: The measure for each target that defines whether it is met

process: Turn each goal into an outcome with a measure. Get fitter becomes resting heart rate or a distance you can cover without stopping.
Keep the list to two or three outcomes. Pursuing every dimension of health at once guarantees none of them gets the minimum dose.
For each target, write the measure you will check and how often, such as a weekly walk time or a monthly strength test.
Confirm each target matters enough to you to sustain for months. A target chosen for appearance alone rarely survives the first dull week.

steps.description: Look up the established minimum dose for each target so you aim at the floor that produces the result, not an arbitrary high bar.

outputs.name: minimum-dose-table
outputs.desc: The minimum effective dose for each target, such as cardio minutes, strength sessions, or mobility minutes per week

outputs.name: dose-source-notes
outputs.desc: A note on where each minimum comes from and any condition that would change it

process: Record the general guidelines. Cardiovascular health responds to roughly one hundred fifty minutes of moderate activity a week. Strength responds to two resistance sessions a week covering the major muscle groups.
Add mobility and recovery minimums where they apply, such as about ten minutes of daily flexibility work and a baseline of sleep that training depends on.
Note that these are population floors. A beginner may see results below the floor, and a specific condition may raise or lower it, so treat the numbers as a starting dose.
Write down the condition under which each minimum would change, so you know when to consult a professional rather than guess.

steps.description: Measure the gap between the minimum dose and what you currently do, so the starting dose is set from reality rather than ambition.

inputs.name: minimum-dose-table
inputs.desc: The minimum dose for each target

inputs.name: current-activity-baseline
inputs.desc: What you currently do in a typical week

outputs.name: current-vs-minimum-gap
outputs.desc: For each target, how far current activity is from the minimum dose

outputs.name: starting-dose
outputs.desc: The dose to begin with, set close to current activity when the gap is large

process: Compare current activity to each minimum. Someone doing zero cardio has a full gap, while someone doing one hundred minutes has only a small one.
Where the gap is large, do not jump straight to the minimum. A jump from zero to one hundred fifty minutes collapses within weeks.
Set the starting dose a step above current activity, not at the final minimum. The first job is to establish the habit, then grow it to the floor.
Where current activity already meets or exceeds the minimum, set the starting dose at maintenance and move attention to another target.

steps.description: Schedule the starting dose into the week in a way you can sustain, because a dose that does not fit the calendar is not a real dose.

inputs.name: minimum-dose-table
inputs.desc: The minimum dose for each target

outputs.name: weekly-dose-schedule
outputs.desc: The starting dose placed into specific days and times across the week

outputs.name: sustainability-check
outputs.desc: A check that the schedule survives a busy week, not just an ideal one

process: Place each dose into specific slots in the week rather than leaving it floating. Scheduled activity happens far more often than intended activity.
Spread the dose to match the target. Two strength sessions sit on separate days with recovery between, and cardio minutes can split across several short sessions.
Run the schedule against a realistic busy week. If it only fits when everything goes right, cut it to a version that fits a hard week.
Build in the smallest fallback version of each session, so a short day still lands a dose rather than a skip.

steps.description: Hold the dose steady for a measurement window and record the metric, so changes to the dose are driven by results rather than impatience.

outputs.name: result-measurements
outputs.desc: The metric for each target recorded across the window at the held dose

outputs.name: below-target-flag
outputs.desc: A flag for each target showing whether the result is at, above, or below the target

process: Hold the dose constant for a window long enough for the body to respond, usually four to six weeks, before judging anything.
Record the metric at the start and end of the window. Changing the dose weekly makes it impossible to tell what caused any change.
Compare the end metric to the target and flag each as at, above, or below. The flag, not a feeling, drives the next step.
Note how sustainable the dose felt. A dose that hit the target but could not be sustained is still a failed dose for the long run.

steps.description: Apply the adjustment rule: increase the dose only when a target is below, and otherwise hold at the minimum that works.

inputs.name: result-measurements
inputs.desc: The recorded metrics at the held dose

inputs.name: below-target-flag
inputs.desc: Whether each target is at, above, or below

outputs.name: dose-adjustment-decision
outputs.desc: For each target, a decision to hold, increase by a small step, or reduce

outputs.name: maintained-minimum
outputs.desc: The sustained dose for targets already being met, protected against creeping upward

process: For any target below its mark, increase the dose by one small step toward or past the minimum, then run another measurement window before increasing again.
For any target at its mark, hold the dose. There is no reward for doing more than the dose that already produces the result, and more adds injury and burnout risk.
For any target above its mark at a high cost in time or fatigue, consider reducing to the smallest dose that still holds the result.
Protect the maintained minimum from drifting upward out of enthusiasm. The method works by finding the floor and staying there, not by always climbing.

description: Diagnose why a behavior change keeps failing using the capability, opportunity, motivation model. Score each of the three, find the lowest, and treat it as the bottleneck. Most people assume the problem is motivation when it is usually opportunity or capability.

steps.description: Frame the specific behavior you are trying to change and gather the history of past attempts, because the history reveals which component keeps failing.

inputs.name: behavior-to-change
inputs.desc: The behavior you keep trying and failing to establish or drop

inputs.name: change-history
inputs.desc: What you have already tried and what happened each time

outputs.name: framed-behavior
outputs.desc: The behavior stated as a single observable action with a context

outputs.name: past-attempt-notes
outputs.desc: A short record of each past attempt and the point at which it broke down

process: State the behavior as one observable action in a context, such as cook dinner at home on weeknights, not eat healthier.
List each past attempt and what specifically ended it. The ending is the clue. Did you not know how, lack the time or tools, or simply not want to in the moment.
Separate the behavior from the goal behind it. The goal may be served by several behaviors, and you are diagnosing one.
Confirm the behavior is within your control. A behavior that depends on another person is diagnosed differently from one that is yours alone.

steps.description: Score your capability to perform the behavior, covering both the physical skill and the psychological knowledge it requires.

inputs.name: framed-behavior
inputs.desc: The behavior stated as an observable action

outputs.name: capability-score
outputs.desc: A score for whether you have the skill, knowledge, and physical ability to do the behavior

outputs.name: capability-evidence
outputs.desc: The specific gaps in skill or knowledge that lower the score

process: Ask whether you actually know how to perform the behavior well. Many diet changes fail because the person cannot cook, not because they lack will.
Separate physical capability from psychological capability. Physical is the body and skill. Psychological is the knowledge, attention, and self-regulation the behavior needs.
Score capability from one to ten, where a low score means you would not know how to do it well even if perfectly motivated and free to act.
Record the specific gaps. Not knowing portion sizes, not knowing proper lifting form, or not having the skill to plan a week are concrete and fixable.

steps.description: Score your opportunity to perform the behavior, covering both the physical environment and the social environment around you.

inputs.name: framed-behavior
inputs.desc: The behavior stated as an observable action

outputs.name: opportunity-score
outputs.desc: A score for whether your time, environment, and social setting allow the behavior

outputs.name: opportunity-evidence
outputs.desc: The specific environmental or social barriers that lower the score

process: Ask whether your environment and schedule physically allow the behavior. Cooking on weeknights is blocked if you get home at nine with no groceries.
Separate physical opportunity from social opportunity. Physical is time, space, money, and tools. Social is whether the people around you make the behavior easy or hard.
Score opportunity from one to ten, where a low score means that even a capable and motivated person would struggle in your current setting.
Record the specific barriers. No time slot, no equipment, a household that eats differently, or a workplace norm are concrete and often changeable.

steps.description: Score your motivation honestly, separating reflective motivation from the automatic pulls that override it in the moment.

inputs.name: framed-behavior
inputs.desc: The behavior stated as an observable action

outputs.name: motivation-score
outputs.desc: A score for how much you actually want the behavior, in reflection and in the moment

outputs.name: motivation-evidence
outputs.desc: Where reflective intention and in-the-moment impulse diverge

process: Separate reflective motivation, what you want when you think it over, from automatic motivation, the habits and impulses that act in the moment.
Score reflective motivation from one to ten. Most people rate this high, which is exactly why they assume motivation is the problem.
Score automatic motivation separately. A person can genuinely want to change yet be pulled by a strong habit loop that fires before reflection arrives.
Record where the two diverge. A large gap between wanting it on reflection and doing the opposite in the moment points to a habit and cue problem, not a desire problem.

steps.description: Compare the three scores and identify the lowest as the bottleneck, because the lowest component is what the behavior is actually waiting on.

outputs.name: lowest-component
outputs.desc: The single component, capability, opportunity, or motivation, with the lowest score

outputs.name: bottleneck-rationale
outputs.desc: Why that component is the constraint and why raising the others would not help yet

process: Lay the three scores side by side. The lowest is the bottleneck, because a behavior cannot happen while any one of the three is missing.
Resist the pull to name motivation by default. If capability or opportunity scored lower, more motivation will only produce more frustrated effort.
Confirm the bottleneck against the past-attempt history. The component that keeps ending the attempts should match the lowest score.
Write why raising the other two would not help yet. Improving a strength that is not the constraint is wasted effort until the bottleneck is addressed.

steps.description: Build an intervention aimed squarely at the bottleneck, and set a trigger to re-diagnose once it is relieved.

inputs.name: bottleneck-rationale
inputs.desc: Why that component is the constraint

outputs.name: intervention-plan
outputs.desc: A plan whose actions all target the bottleneck component directly

outputs.name: reassessment-trigger
outputs.desc: The condition under which you re-score all three components to find the new bottleneck

process: Match the intervention to the bottleneck. A capability bottleneck needs instruction and practice. An opportunity bottleneck needs environment and schedule changes. A motivation bottleneck needs cue and habit work or a stronger reason.
Direct every action in the plan at the bottleneck. Adding unrelated improvements dilutes the effort and obscures whether the fix worked.
Set the reassessment trigger, such as once capability reaches a six, re-score all three. Relieving one bottleneck usually reveals a new one.
Plan to run the whole diagnostic again after the trigger fires, because the constraint moves as the behavior develops.

description: Protect a habit with the rule never miss twice. Missing once is data, missing twice is the start of a new pattern. After a miss, do a scaled-down version the next day, such as two pushups or one written sentence, to preserve both the identity and the pattern.

steps.description: Define the habit you intend to sustain as a streak and record how consistent it is right now.

inputs.name: habit-to-sustain
inputs.desc: The habit you want to keep going without long breaks

inputs.name: current-consistency
inputs.desc: How often you currently manage it in a typical week

outputs.name: defined-streak-habit
outputs.desc: The habit stated as a single daily or near-daily action that can carry a streak

outputs.name: streak-baseline
outputs.desc: The current longest run and typical gap length for the habit

process: State the habit as one action that recurs often enough to form a streak, such as a daily walk or a daily page of writing.
Record the current baseline honestly: the longest run you have managed and how long the gaps between runs tend to be.
Confirm the habit is one you want daily or near daily. A habit meant to happen twice a week uses a different rule than a daily streak.
Note what a single rep of the habit normally costs in time and effort, because the recovery version will be a fraction of it.

steps.description: Set the never miss twice rule and define exactly what counts as a miss, so the rule is unambiguous under pressure.

inputs.name: streak-baseline
inputs.desc: The current run and gap pattern

outputs.name: never-miss-twice-rule
outputs.desc: The written rule that one miss is allowed but a second consecutive miss is not

outputs.name: miss-definition
outputs.desc: A precise definition of what counts as a miss and what counts as a completed day

process: Write the rule plainly: one missed day is acceptable, but you will never miss two days in a row. The second miss is where a streak turns into a lapse.
Define a miss precisely. Decide the minimum that counts as a completed day, so you are never arguing with yourself about whether a partial day counts.
Frame a single miss as data, not failure. One miss tells you something about your week. Treating it as failure is what triggers the spiral into a second and third.
Separate the streak from perfection. The goal is to never let the gap reach two, not to achieve an unbroken record, because perfectionism ends streaks the fastest.

steps.description: Design the scaled-down recovery version of the habit, small enough that it is always possible on the day after a miss.

outputs.name: scaled-down-version
outputs.desc: A tiny version of the habit, such as two pushups or one sentence, used after a miss

outputs.name: recovery-trigger
outputs.desc: The rule that the scaled-down version is performed the day after any miss, without exception

process: Shrink the habit to a version so small it cannot be refused, such as two pushups, one written sentence, or a five-minute walk.
The recovery version exists to preserve the pattern and the identity, not to produce results. Showing up tiny keeps the chain from breaking.
Write the recovery trigger: the day after any miss, you do at least the scaled-down version, whatever else happens that day.
Make the recovery version require no preparation, so it is available on exactly the kind of bad day that caused the first miss.

steps.description: Set up a log that records misses and counts consecutive misses, so the second miss is impossible to ignore.

outputs.name: miss-log
outputs.desc: A simple record marking each day as completed, recovery, or miss

outputs.name: consecutive-miss-counter
outputs.desc: A running count of consecutive misses that resets on any completed or recovery day

process: Mark every day as completed, recovery, or miss. Three states, not two, so a recovery day is visibly different from a full day and from a miss.
Keep a consecutive-miss counter that increments on a miss and resets to zero on any completed or recovery day.
Place the log where you will see it daily, because the point is to catch the counter at one before it reaches two.
Review the misses for patterns over time. Misses that cluster on the same weekday or situation reveal a design problem to fix at the source.

steps.description: Plan exactly how the recovery version is executed when the counter hits one, so recovery is automatic rather than a decision.

outputs.name: recovery-action-plan
outputs.desc: The concrete steps to perform the recovery version the day after a miss

outputs.name: identity-preservation-note
outputs.desc: A reminder that completing the recovery version keeps the identity intact despite the miss

process: Write the recovery as a concrete sequence for the day after a miss, so when the counter reads one you execute rather than deliberate.
Lower the bar to the recovery version, not the full habit. Trying to make up for a miss with a double session usually produces another skip.
Attach the recovery to a fixed moment the next day, so it has a reliable slot rather than waiting for motivation that may not come.
Write the identity note: a person who recovers the next day is still that kind of person. The recovery day is proof the identity survived the miss.

steps.description: Review the log to confirm the never miss twice rule is holding and adjust the protocol where double misses still slip through.

inputs.name: miss-log
inputs.desc: The record of completed, recovery, and miss days

outputs.name: pattern-integrity-report
outputs.desc: A summary of how often the rule held and how quickly recoveries happened

outputs.name: protocol-adjustment
outputs.desc: Changes to the recovery version, triggers, or habit size where double misses occurred

process: Count the double misses. Zero or very few means the protocol is holding. Several means the recovery version is still too large or the trigger is unreliable.
Check how fast recoveries happened. A miss followed immediately by a recovery day is the intended pattern. A miss followed by another miss needs a smaller recovery version.
For any cluster of double misses, trace the cause. A recurring hard day may need its own smaller default rather than relying on recovery after the fact.
Adjust the smallest lever that fixes it. Usually shrinking the recovery version or fixing its trigger restores the pattern without touching the main habit.

description: Design sleep around a fixed wake time held even on weekends. Count back seven to eight hours to find bedtime, then build a wind-down that dims lights ninety minutes before, keeps the room between sixty-five and sixty-eight degrees, stops screens sixty minutes before, and cuts caffeine by early afternoon. Track quality, not only duration.

steps.description: Set a single fixed wake time to be held every day including weekends, because the wake time anchors the entire sleep rhythm.

inputs.name: current-sleep-pattern
inputs.desc: Your current bedtimes, wake times, and how much they vary day to day

inputs.name: daily-obligations
inputs.desc: The fixed demands on your mornings, such as work or family start times

outputs.name: fixed-wake-time
outputs.desc: A single wake time to hold every day of the week

outputs.name: wake-time-rationale
outputs.desc: Why that time fits your obligations and can be held on weekends

process: Choose the wake time from your least flexible morning. The wake time must work on the day with the earliest fixed demand, then apply to every other day too.
Commit to holding it on weekends within about an hour. Sleeping in shifts the body clock and recreates the Monday morning difficulty every week.
Confirm the wake time leaves room for seven to eight hours of sleep at a bedtime you could realistically keep.
Write why this time is sustainable. A wake time chosen from ambition rather than obligation will not survive, and an unstable wake time undoes everything downstream.

steps.description: Count back from the fixed wake time to find the target bedtime and the full sleep window.

inputs.name: sleep-need-estimate
inputs.desc: Your estimated nightly sleep need, usually seven to eight hours

outputs.name: target-bedtime
outputs.desc: The bedtime that yields the needed sleep given the fixed wake time

outputs.name: sleep-window
outputs.desc: The protected window from target bedtime to wake time

process: Subtract your sleep need from the fixed wake time to find the target bedtime. A seven o'clock wake with an eight-hour need sets an eleven o'clock bedtime.
Add a short buffer for falling asleep, usually fifteen to twenty minutes, so the window reflects time in bed, not only time asleep.
Treat the resulting window as protected time. The sleep window is a scheduled appointment, not whatever is left after the day ends.
If the target bedtime is impossible given your evenings, the wake time or the obligations must change. Do not solve it by cutting the sleep need below your real need.

steps.description: Design the wind-down sequence that leads into the sleep window, dimming light early and ending screens well before bedtime.

outputs.name: winddown-sequence
outputs.desc: An ordered sequence of wind-down actions tied to times before bedtime

outputs.name: winddown-start-time
outputs.desc: The time the wind-down begins, roughly ninety minutes before bedtime

process: Set the wind-down to begin about ninety minutes before bedtime, and dim the lights at that point. Bright light late tells the body clock it is still day.
Stop screens about sixty minutes before bedtime, or at minimum cut their brightness and blue light, because screen light and stimulation both delay sleep onset.
Fill the wind-down with low-arousal actions in a consistent order, such as tidying, washing, and reading on paper, so the sequence itself becomes a sleep cue.
Keep the sequence short enough to hold on a normal night. A wind-down that demands a perfect evening will be abandoned on the first busy one.

steps.description: Specify the bedroom conditions that support sleep, centered on a cool, dark, quiet room.

inputs.name: current-sleep-pattern
inputs.desc: Your current sleep conditions and disruptions

outputs.name: environment-settings
outputs.desc: The target bedroom settings for temperature, light, and noise

outputs.name: environment-change-list
outputs.desc: The specific changes needed to reach those settings

process: Set the room temperature between about sixty-five and sixty-eight degrees. A cool room supports the drop in body temperature that sleep onset depends on.
Make the room as dark as practical with blackout cover or a mask, and remove or cover small light sources that interrupt sleep.
Address noise with steady background sound or ear protection if the environment is unpredictable, since sudden noises fragment sleep even when they do not wake you fully.
List the concrete changes needed, such as a thermostat schedule, a blackout cover, or moving a device out of the room, and treat them as one-time fixes.

steps.description: Set cutoff times for caffeine and other stimulants so they do not undermine the sleep window hours later.

outputs.name: caffeine-cutoff-time
outputs.desc: The time after which no caffeine is consumed, usually early afternoon

outputs.name: stimulant-rules
outputs.desc: Rules for other sleep-disrupting inputs such as alcohol, heavy meals, and late intense exercise

process: Set a caffeine cutoff in the early afternoon, around eight hours before bedtime, because caffeine has a long half-life and lingers well into the evening.
Add rules for alcohol. It may bring on drowsiness but it fragments the second half of the night, so keep it away from the hours before bed.
Set a cutoff for heavy meals and for intense exercise, both of which raise arousal and body temperature and push sleep onset later when done too close to bed.
Keep the rules simple enough to remember, anchored to clock times, so they are easy to follow without tracking every input.

steps.description: Track sleep quality and not only hours, because time in bed does not equal restorative sleep.

outputs.name: quality-tracker
outputs.desc: A daily log of sleep quality markers, not just duration

outputs.name: quality-vs-duration-metrics
outputs.desc: A view of how rested you feel relative to hours spent in bed

process: Log duration, but add quality markers: how long it took to fall asleep, how many times you woke, and how rested you felt on waking.
Record a simple morning rating of alertness. Feeling unrested after eight hours is a quality problem that duration alone would hide.
Watch for the mismatch between long time in bed and poor rest. That gap points to fragmented sleep from environment, stimulants, or stress rather than too little time.
Keep the log light enough to sustain, a few marks each morning, so it survives past the first enthusiastic week.

steps.description: Review the quality data against the design and adjust the element that is holding sleep back.

inputs.name: quality-vs-duration-metrics
inputs.desc: Rested feeling relative to time in bed

outputs.name: protocol-review-summary
outputs.desc: A summary of which sleep markers improved and which did not

outputs.name: sleep-protocol-adjustment
outputs.desc: The single change to make next, aimed at the weakest marker

process: Read the markers after two to three weeks. Judge each one separately: onset time, awakenings, and morning alertness can move independently.

Trace a weak marker to its likely cause. Slow onset points to light or stimulants, frequent awakenings point to environment or alcohol, and unrested mornings with full hours point to quality disruption.
Change one element at a time. Adjusting several at once makes it impossible to tell which change helped.
Protect the fixed wake time through every adjustment. It is the anchor, and loosening it to chase a quick fix undoes the whole design.

description: Match the response to the type of stress. Acute stress needs a physiological reset such as box breathing, cold water, or a walk. Chronic stress needs a structural change that reduces the source. Anticipatory stress needs cognitive defusion: name it, write it down, and set a time to address it.

steps.description: Log recent stress episodes and their triggers, because the right response depends on knowing what kind of stress each one is.

inputs.name: recent-stress-episodes
inputs.desc: Specific moments of stress over the past week or two

inputs.name: stress-triggers
inputs.desc: What tended to set each episode off

outputs.name: stress-log
outputs.desc: A record of each episode with its trigger, intensity, and how it resolved

outputs.name: trigger-list
outputs.desc: The recurring triggers that appear across episodes

process: Record each stress episode with what triggered it, how intense it was, and how long it lasted. Do this close to the event while the detail is fresh.
Note how each episode resolved. Did it pass on its own, did something you did help, or did it linger and color the whole day.
Pull out the triggers that recur. A trigger that appears repeatedly is a candidate for a structural fix rather than repeated in-the-moment coping.
Keep the log plain and quick. The aim is enough detail to classify the stress, not a full journal that becomes its own burden.

steps.description: Classify each logged episode as acute, chronic, or anticipatory, because each type responds to a different tool.

outputs.name: classified-stressors
outputs.desc: Each episode and trigger tagged as acute, chronic, or anticipatory

outputs.name: type-distribution
outputs.desc: The share of your stress that falls into each type

process: Tag acute stress: a sharp spike tied to a specific event that passes, such as a near miss in traffic or a tense exchange.
Tag chronic stress: a steady background load from an ongoing source, such as an overloaded schedule, a strained relationship, or money pressure.
Tag anticipatory stress: worry about something that has not happened yet, such as a looming deadline, conversation, or appointment.
Tally the distribution. A person mostly carrying chronic stress needs structural change, while one spiking on acute events needs reset tools, and the mix tells you where to invest.

steps.description: Assemble physiological reset tools for acute stress, the kind that calm the body quickly in the moment.

inputs.name: type-distribution
inputs.desc: The share of each stress type

outputs.name: acute-reset-tools
outputs.desc: A short set of fast physiological resets such as box breathing, cold water, and a brisk walk

outputs.name: acute-use-cues
outputs.desc: The body signals that tell you to reach for a reset tool

process: Choose two or three resets that act on the body directly. Box breathing slows the heart, cold water on the face triggers a calming reflex, and a brisk walk discharges the stress response.
Acute stress is physiological first, so the fastest path down is through the body, not through reasoning about the situation.
Define the cues that should trigger a reset, such as a racing heart, shallow breathing, or clenched muscles. The cue is what tells you to use the tool before the spike peaks.
Practice the resets when calm so they are available under stress. A tool you have never rehearsed will not come to mind in the moment you need it.

steps.description: Plan structural changes for chronic stress, because a background load does not respond to in-the-moment tools and must be reduced at the source.

inputs.name: type-distribution
inputs.desc: The share of each stress type

outputs.name: chronic-source-plan
outputs.desc: A plan to reduce or remove the ongoing sources of chronic stress

outputs.name: structural-changes
outputs.desc: The specific changes to schedule, environment, commitments, or relationships that lower the load

process: List the ongoing sources behind the chronic stress. Chronic stress comes from a situation that keeps generating it, not from a single event.
For each source, ask what structural change would reduce it: removing a commitment, renegotiating a demand, changing an environment, or setting a boundary.
Accept that reset tools only mask chronic stress. Breathing exercises do not fix an overloaded schedule, and relying on them lets the source grind on.
Pick the one or two changes with the largest effect and plan them concretely, since chronic load usually traces back to a small number of big sources.

steps.description: Build a defusion protocol for anticipatory stress: name the worry, write it down, and set a specific time to deal with it.

inputs.name: type-distribution
inputs.desc: The share of each stress type

outputs.name: defusion-protocol
outputs.desc: The steps to name and externalize an anticipatory worry so it stops looping

outputs.name: scheduled-worry-time
outputs.desc: A set time to actually address the worry, which lets the mind release it until then

process: Name the worry explicitly. Anticipatory stress loops because it stays vague, and naming it as a specific concern shrinks it from a cloud to a defined item.
Write it down to get it out of your head. An externalized worry stops demanding to be rehearsed to avoid being forgotten.
Schedule a specific time to address it, so the mind can let go of it now knowing it has a slot. An unscheduled worry keeps resurfacing to make sure it is not lost.
At the scheduled time, decide one concrete next action on the worry. Often the action is small, and taking it ends the anticipation that was heavier than the task.

steps.description: Build a single guide that routes each kind of stress to the right tool, so the response is matched rather than random.

outputs.name: stress-response-matcher
outputs.desc: A guide mapping each stress type to its matched response

outputs.name: quick-reference-card
outputs.desc: A short card you can reach for in the moment to pick the right tool fast

process: Write the matching rule: acute goes to a physiological reset, chronic goes to a structural change, anticipatory goes to defusion and a scheduled time.
Put the rule on a short reference card. In a stressed moment you need a quick route to the right tool, not a long document to read.
Flag the common mismatch: using a reset tool on chronic stress. It feels productive but leaves the source untouched, so the card should prompt you to check the type first.
Keep the card where stress tends to hit, so the matched response is close at hand rather than remembered only after the episode has passed.

steps.description: Review the toolkit against the stress log to see which responses worked and refine the weak ones.

inputs.name: stress-log
inputs.desc: The ongoing record of stress episodes

outputs.name: effectiveness-review
outputs.desc: A summary of which matched responses reduced stress and which did not

outputs.name: toolkit-refinement
outputs.desc: Changes to tools, cues, or the structural plan where the response fell short

process: Compare recent episodes to earlier ones. A working toolkit shows acute spikes resolving faster and chronic load easing as sources are reduced.
For each type, judge whether the matched response actually helped. An acute reset that never gets used in time points to a cue problem, not a tool problem.
If chronic stress has not eased, check whether the structural change was actually made. Chronic load does not fall until the source changes, no matter how good the acute tools are.
Refine the weakest part. Usually it is a missing cue, a reset not yet practiced, or a structural change that was planned but never executed.

description: Build a health maintenance system for the year. Schedule checkups appropriate to your age and risk, record baseline numbers, track changes year over year, and place daily, weekly, monthly, and annual routines on the calendar so maintenance happens by schedule rather than by crisis.

steps.description: Build a profile of your age and risk factors, because the right checkups and routines depend on both.

inputs.name: age-and-sex
inputs.desc: Your age and sex, which set the baseline screening calendar

inputs.name: personal-and-family-history
inputs.desc: Your own conditions and the conditions that run in your family

outputs.name: risk-profile
outputs.desc: A profile combining age-based baseline risk with your personal and family history

outputs.name: risk-flags
outputs.desc: The specific elevated risks that call for earlier or more frequent screening

process: Start from age and sex, which set the standard screening calendar most guidelines are organized around.
Layer in personal history: existing conditions, past results, and current measures that raise or lower risk.
Layer in family history, flagging conditions that appeared in close relatives, since these often move a screening earlier or make it more frequent.
Mark the risk flags clearly. These are the points where your calendar will differ from the standard one, and they drive the schedule in the next step.

steps.description: Build the screening and checkup schedule from the risk profile, placing each appointment on a calendar rather than leaving it to memory.

inputs.name: risk-flags
inputs.desc: The elevated risks needing earlier screening

outputs.name: screening-schedule
outputs.desc: The set of checkups and screenings with their recommended intervals

outputs.name: checkup-calendar
outputs.desc: The schedule placed onto actual dates for the coming year

process: List the standard checkups for your profile, such as an annual physical, dental visits, vision checks, and the age-appropriate screenings for your profile.
Adjust intervals for each risk flag. An elevated risk may move a screening earlier or make it more frequent than the standard interval.
Confirm anything beyond the routine with a clinician. The system schedules and tracks care, it does not replace the judgment of a professional about what you specifically need.
Place each appointment on actual dates across the year, spacing them so they do not all fall in one month, and treat the dates as booked commitments.

steps.description: Record your baseline health numbers now, so future changes can be measured against a known starting point.

outputs.name: baseline-numbers
outputs.desc: The current values of your key health measures

outputs.name: metric-tracking-sheet
outputs.desc: A sheet that holds each measure with room for yearly values

process: Record the measures that matter for your profile, such as blood pressure, resting heart rate, key blood values, weight, and anything tied to a risk flag.
Capture the current value and the date for each. A number without a date cannot be compared cleanly against next year.
Build a tracking sheet with one row per measure and a column per year, so the record grows into a trend rather than a scatter of readings.
Note the healthy range for each measure beside its value, so a reading can be read in context rather than in isolation.

steps.description: Design the daily, weekly, monthly, and annual routines that maintain health between checkups, and place them on the calendar.

outputs.name: routine-cadence-plan
outputs.desc: Health routines sorted into daily, weekly, monthly, and annual cadences

outputs.name: calendar-entries
outputs.desc: The routines placed as recurring calendar entries

process: Sort maintenance into cadences. Daily routines cover movement, sleep, and hydration. Weekly routines cover planning and heavier training. Monthly routines cover self-checks and reviews. Annual routines cover the scheduled screenings.
Match each routine to the cadence that fits its purpose, so nothing that needs daily attention is left to a monthly review.
Place the recurring routines on the calendar as entries, so maintenance runs on a schedule rather than waiting for a symptom to force it.
Keep each cadence light enough to sustain. A maintenance system overloaded with daily tasks collapses, and the point is steady routine, not maximum effort.

steps.description: Set up year over year tracking of the baseline numbers so slow changes become visible before they become problems.

inputs.name: metric-tracking-sheet
inputs.desc: The sheet holding each measure by year

outputs.name: trend-tracker
outputs.desc: A view of each measure across years that shows direction, not just the latest value

outputs.name: change-alert-rules
outputs.desc: Rules for how much change in a measure should prompt attention or a clinician visit

process: Record each measure in the same way every year, so the comparison reflects real change rather than differences in how it was taken.
Read each measure as a direction across years, not a single reading. A value drifting steadily toward the edge of its range matters even while it is still in range.
Set alert rules for meaningful change, so a measure moving by a defined amount prompts a closer look rather than being noticed only once it is far out of range.
Keep the trend view simple enough to scan each year, since a record you cannot read quickly will not get read.

steps.description: Define an annual review that reads the trends, confirms the screenings happened, and resets the system for the coming year.

inputs.name: trend-tracker
inputs.desc: The year over year view of measures

outputs.name: annual-review-checklist
outputs.desc: A checklist for the yearly review of trends, screenings, and routines

outputs.name: review-date
outputs.desc: A fixed date each year to run the review

process: Set a fixed annual date for the review, such as around a birthday, so it recurs without needing to be remembered.
On the checklist, read the trend tracker for any measure moving the wrong way and confirm every scheduled screening actually happened.
Add the new year of numbers to the tracking sheet during the review, so the record stays current and the trend extends by one year.
Confirm the routines still fit the coming year. Age, conditions, and circumstances change, and the system should be reset to match rather than run unchanged.

steps.description: Adjust the system for the coming year based on the review, updating screenings, routines, and alert rules as risk changes.

inputs.name: trend-tracker
inputs.desc: The year over year view of measures

outputs.name: system-adjustment-plan
outputs.desc: The changes to screenings, routines, and alert rules for the coming year

outputs.name: next-year-targets
outputs.desc: The specific measures or routines to focus on in the year ahead

process: Update the screening schedule for any new risk flags the year revealed, moving screenings earlier or adding them where trends warrant, confirmed with a clinician.
Adjust the routines to address the measures trending the wrong way, so the daily and weekly cadence targets the actual risk rather than a generic one.
Revise the alert rules where a measure has moved, so next year's thresholds reflect your current starting point rather than last year's.
Name a small number of focus targets for the year, since a system that tries to improve everything at once tends to hold nothing, and a few targets keep the effort real.
